Reproductive allocation in Treadfin butterflyfish was assessed through field collections conducted near the Great Barrier Reef during the austral summer spawning period. Dissections of gravid females showed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This moderate investment in ovarian tissue relative to somatic mass suggests a strategy of repeated, low-effort spawning events rather than a single, high-output pulse. The timing of these events appears tightly linked to thermal conditions, as the index declines markedly in cooler months when temperatures fall below this threshold. Field observations indicate that females actively spawn from October through March, releasing small batches of pelagic eggs on a near-daily basis during peak periods.

Total body length in fully grown individuals of Chaetodon auriga typically reaches 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a size that is consistent with the mid-range of body sizes observed across the Chaetodontidae. This ultimate length is attained gradually over several years of sustained somatic growth, with most individuals reaching asymptotic size by approximately their fifth or sixth year of life. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight regressions for this species, is approximately 368 grams [Wwi = approximately 368 grams], placing it among the heavier butterflyfishes in its guild. Such a body mass supports an active foraging lifestyle on the coral reef, where adults use their elongated snouts to extract polyps and small invertebrates from crevices. The length-weight relationship itself follows the typical allometric scaling for teleosts, reflecting a robust, laterally compressed body form that facilitates maneuverability in complex reef habitats.

Sexual maturation in the Treadfin butterflyfish is marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, which field studies show begins when individuals reach approximately 13 centimeters [Lp = approximately 13 centimeters] in total length. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is roughly 52.4 grams [Wwp = roughly 52.4 grams], indicating that roughly one-seventh of the ultimate body mass is achieved before reproductive capability is attained. This relatively early maturation relative to final size is common among reef fishes that experience high adult mortality and thus benefit from an earlier onset of breeding. Histological examination of gonadal tissues from specimens at this length confirms the presence of developing oocytes or active spermatogenesis, providing firm evidence of functional reproductive status. The transition from immature juvenile to pubertal adult thus occurs well before full somatic growth is completed, a pattern consistent with an income-breeding strategy on productive coral reefs.

Early life history events in Chaetodon auriga occur rapidly under warm thermal regimes typical of tropical reef environments. At a rearing temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], embryonic development proceeds quickly, and the age at birth—defined as the moment of eclosion when the chorion ruptures and the yolk-sac larva emerges—is approximately 1.25 days [ab = approximately 1.25 days] following egg fertilisation. This rapid hatching time is characteristic of small, pelagic eggs that are vulnerable to predation and require swift progression to a free-swimming larval stage. The wet weight at birth, based on an egg diameter of 0.75 millimeters for the congener Chaetodon larvatus, is calculated at 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], reflecting the minute size of the newly emerged larva. These yolk-sac larvae remain entirely endotrophic for the first several days, relying on endogenous reserves before their mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. The combination of swift hatching and small initial size represents a classic life-history trade-off between rapid development and the production of numerous, poorly provisioned offspring.

Longevity records for the Treadfin butterflyfish indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] under natural field conditions at the average annual water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a duration that places it among the longer-lived members of the Chaetodontidae. This considerable lifespan reflects the species' occupation of stable coral reef habitats where predation risk is moderate and food resources are seasonally predictable. Such extended longevity allows for repeated reproductive effort across many breeding seasons, a strategy that buffers against years of poor recruitment. In comparison to smaller, more short-lived butterflyfishes that complete their life cycle in under a decade, Chaetodon auriga exhibits a distinctly slower pace of life, with later maturity and higher survival rates among adults.
